# METHODOLOGY

This chapter explains how the study answers its research questions. It describes how the posts are collected and annotated, how the models are trained and compared, and how the benchmarking system and the prototype web application are built and tested.

## Research Methodology

This study follows the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) of Peffers et al. [-@peffers2007design]. Design science research creates and evaluates artifacts intended to solve identified problems [@peffers2007design]. The methodology fits this study because its main contribution is an artifact, a multi-task model that performs humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts. The dataset on which the model is trained, a set of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both tasks, is a second artifact.

DSRM consists of six activities, and the study carries them out in order [@peffers2007design]. The first two, identifying the problem and defining the objectives of a solution, are presented in Chapter 1. The third is design and development. In this activity, the dataset is built, the multi-task model is designed, and one of 13 multi-task optimizers is selected on the validation set. The candidate multi-task model trained with the selected optimizer is the final multi-task model. The fourth activity is demonstration, in which the final multi-task model is used in a prototype web application. The fifth is evaluation, in which the final multi-task model is compared on the test set with two single-task models, one for each task. The agreement between the annotators is also measured to check how consistently the dataset is annotated. The sixth is communication. The results are reported in this thesis, and the final multi-task model, the code, and the post IDs of the dataset are released.

## Subjects of the Study

The subjects of this study are the dataset, the multi-task model, and the two single-task models that serve as baselines. The dataset consists of about 2,500 Taglish posts on X about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. Each post is given one of the 10 humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid], listed in @tbl-categories. The entity spans in the post are marked with the 10 entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], listed in @tbl-entity-types. HUMAID-NER uses the same categories and entity types, so each F1-score of this study has a counterpart in HUMAID-NER. The comparison is only approximate, because HUMAID-NER is in English, is much larger, and has a similar number of posts in each category (Section 1.8).

The multi-task model follows the design of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. A single pretrained transformer encoder reads the post, and two task heads use its output, one to assign the humanitarian category and one to mark the entity spans (@fig-artifact). Each head is trained with a cross-entropy loss. This design is hard parameter sharing (Section 2.2). The encoder is SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which is chosen because it was pretrained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion].

The multi-task model is trained with 13 multi-task optimizers, listed in @tbl-optimizers. Each optimizer gives one candidate multi-task model, so there are 13 candidate multi-task models. The optimizers are selected using two criteria. First, an optimizer must have been evaluated in at least two of the seven empirical studies of multi-task optimizers reviewed in Chapter 2. Requiring two studies limits the comparison to well-established optimizers, following Kurin et al. [-@kurin2022unitary]. Second, an optimizer must be trainable with the same model and training setup as the others, so that the optimizer is the only difference among the candidate multi-task models. No other optimizer in these studies meets both criteria.

Each single-task model is trained on one task alone. It uses the same encoder as the candidate multi-task models and the same task head and loss for its task. In total, 15 models are trained, the 13 candidate multi-task models and the two single-task models.

## Sampling Technique

The sampling frame consists of the posts on X that match the search keywords and fall within the collection window of a tropical cyclone. Each window starts one day before the tropical cyclone entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility and ends three days after it left. The dates of entry and exit are taken from the preliminary tropical cyclone reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. The window extends beyond these dates because people also post about a tropical cyclone before it arrives and after it leaves. Zou et al. [-@zou2025typhoon] likewise collected posts from two days before to four days after landfall. Fewer extra days are added in this study because a tropical cyclone is already approaching the country while it is within the Philippine Area of Responsibility.

The search keywords are *bagyo* (tropical cyclone), *baha* (flood), and words formed from these two Tagalog roots, such as *bagyong* and *pagbaha* (@tbl-keyword-forms). The search function of X compares a keyword with the separate words of a post [@x2026operators]. A search for *bagyo* does not return a post that contains only *bagyong*, so every word form is searched as a separate keyword. Storm names are not used as keywords, because many local storm names are also personal names and match far more posts than the keywords do (@tbl-storm-names).

A post is included when it contains at least one English word and at least one Tagalog word. The language of each word is identified with the dictionary-based method of Herrera et al. [-@herrera2022tweettaglish], which was developed for Taglish posts on X. One word of each language is enough, because any higher minimum would be arbitrary.

Reposts, quotes, and duplicates are excluded. A repost repeats a post that is already in the frame, and a quote includes text written by another user. Exact and near duplicates repeat the same text, which would then be counted more than once and could appear in both the training set and the test set. Duplicates are identified with the method of HumAID [@alam2021humaid], which measures how much wording two posts share (@tbl-duplicate-steps). When the similarity of two posts exceeds 0.75, only one of them is kept. HumAID adopted this threshold from @alam2021crisisbench, who set it after manually checking posts at several thresholds.

About 2,500 posts are drawn for annotation by proportionate stratified random sampling. Each day is a stratum, and it contributes posts in proportion to its number of matching posts. Simple random sampling would require the full list of matching posts, which is too costly to retrieve. Stratifying by humanitarian category is not possible either, because the category of a post is known only after annotation. The sample is limited to about 2,500 posts because that is the most that two annotators can complete at 2 to 3 hours a day over the 38 working days from December 2026 to January 2027. This is a sample size based on resource constraints [@lakens2022sample].

The annotated posts are divided into a training set (72%), a validation set (14%), and a test set (14%), following the proportions of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. Every model is trained, validated, and tested on the same posts, so that differences between models cannot come from differences in the posts. The split is stratified by humanitarian category, so each category has approximately the same share in all three sets. A category with too few posts to appear in all three sets is kept entirely in the training set, is left out of macro-F1, and is reported as a limitation. It is not merged with another category, because merged categories could no longer be compared with those of HUMAID-NER.

## Instruments to Be Used

Inter-annotator agreement on the humanitarian categories is measured with Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960coefficient]. Two annotators can assign the same category to a post by chance alone, so kappa removes the agreement expected by chance from the proportion of posts on which the annotators agree. A kappa of 1 means complete agreement, and a kappa of 0 means no more agreement than chance. Agreement is computed only for the categories, because the entity spans are annotated automatically by GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner].

Model performance refers to how correctly a model assigns humanitarian categories and marks entity spans. It is evaluated with the F1-score, which compares a model's predictions with the annotated categories and the GLiNER spans. Accuracy is not used, because the categories differ in their number of posts and a model can reach a high accuracy by favoring the most frequent categories. The F1-score combines two proportions. Precision is the proportion of a model's predictions that are correct, and recall is the proportion of the annotated items that the model finds. For a humanitarian category or an entity type $c$,
$$P_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FP_c}, \qquad R_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c}, \qquad F1_c = \frac{2 P_c R_c}{P_c + R_c}$$
where $TP_c$ is the number of correct predictions of $c$, $FP_c$ is the number of incorrect predictions of $c$, $FN_c$ is the number of instances of $c$ that the model fails to predict, and $P_c$ and $R_c$ are precision and recall.

Humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, the mean of $F1_c$ over the 10 categories. Macro-F1 gives rare categories the same weight as frequent ones. A category that is kept entirely in the training set (Section 3.3) is not part of this mean. NER is scored with span-level micro-F1, which pools the counts of all 10 entity types before the formula is applied. A predicted span counts as correct only when both its boundaries and its type match those of an annotated span. Both scores are computed as in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner].

Negative transfer occurs when a multi-task model has a lower F1-score on a task than the model trained on that task alone. It is measured as the percentage by which the F1-score of a candidate multi-task model is higher or lower than that of the single-task model. This relative change in F1-score is a widely used measure of multi-task performance [@vandenhende2022dense; @gama2026uniform]. It is computed for each task $t$ and averaged over the two tasks,
$$\Delta_t = \frac{F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t} - F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}}{F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}} \times 100\%, \qquad \Delta_{\text{MTL}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_1 + \Delta_2\right)$$
where task 1 is humanitarian classification and task 2 is NER. Here, $F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t}$ is the F1-score of one run of a candidate multi-task model, and $F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}$ is the mean F1-score over the five runs of the single-task model for task $t$. For example, when a candidate multi-task model reaches an F1-score of 0.76 on a task and the single-task model reaches 0.80, $\Delta_t$ is −5%. A negative $\Delta_t$ indicates negative transfer on task $t$, and a positive $\Delta_t$ indicates positive transfer.

Training time is the time, in seconds, that a run spends on training steps. Peak memory is the largest amount of graphics processing unit (GPU) memory, in mebibytes, that PyTorch allocates at any moment of the run. One multi-task model replaces both single-task models, so its training time is compared with the sum of the training times of the two single-task models. Its peak memory is compared with the larger of their two peak memories, because the single-task models are trained one after the other. The overhead of an optimizer is the percentage by which the training time or peak memory of its candidate multi-task model exceeds that of the model trained with equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary; @liu2023famo].

## Procedure of Data Gathering

Posts are collected through the X API, which charges US\$0.005 for each post that it returns, including posts that are later excluded [@x2026pricing]. The keywords match 176,424 posts in the collection windows (@tbl-frame-counts), so retrieving all of them would cost about US\$882. To avoid this cost, the posts are collected in two steps. First, only the number of matching posts on each day is requested, and these numbers set how many posts each day contributes to the sample. Second, the posts of each day are retrieved and filtered by the inclusion and exclusion criteria until the day has contributed its number of posts (@tbl-collection-steps). The 2,500 posts cost at least US\$12.50, and the final cost depends on how many of the retrieved posts are eligible. When fewer than 2,500 eligible posts are found, all eligible posts are annotated, and the smaller dataset is reported as a limitation.

Users of X keep ownership of their posts but grant X a license to make the posts available to others [@x2026terms]. The study receives the posts through the X API under this license, so users are not asked individually for consent. The personal information in the posts is still protected. Usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and links are replaced with placeholders, because these details can identify a person and are not needed for either task. Names within the text of a post are kept, because PERSON is one of the entity types. The posts are stored only on the laptop used for training, and only the research group and the adjudicator have access to them. These measures follow Section 20 of the Data Privacy Act [-@philippines2012dataprivacy], which requires reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against unlawful access and disclosure. As the developer policy of X requires, posts deleted on X are also deleted from the dataset, and only the post IDs are shared [@x2026devpolicy].

Two annotators assign the humanitarian category of every post in the annotation tool doccano. Both are members of the research group and are fluent in Tagalog and English. An adjudicator from outside the research group, who works or does research in disaster management or crisis informatics, decides the disagreements that the annotators cannot settle. @tbl-annotators lists the qualifications and tasks of the annotators and the adjudicator.

Annotation begins with practice batches of 50 posts. These posts are collected in the same way as the sample but are not part of it, so that no post in the sample is seen before the guidelines are fixed. After each practice batch, Cohen's kappa is computed and the guidelines in Appendix A are revised. Practice ends when kappa reaches at least .61, the lower bound of substantial agreement [@landis1977measurement], or after the third practice batch. When kappa is still below .61 after the third batch, annotation of the sample begins, and the agreement is reported as it is. The practice batches are annotated before December 2026, so they take no time from the 38 working days.

The guidelines are then fixed, and the sample is annotated from December 2026 to January 2027 in eight batches of about 310 posts, following the rules in @tbl-annotation-rules. At the planned pace of about 66 posts a day, one batch is about one working week of annotation, so agreement is measured every week. Kappa is computed for each batch from the annotations that the two annotators make independently, before any discussion. The annotators then settle their disagreements by discussion. The adjudicator decides the disagreements that remain and signs off on the batch. When the kappa of a batch falls below .61, the annotators and the adjudicator also review the guidelines and the disagreements of that batch before the next batch begins. The batch is not annotated again, because the 38 working days leave no time to repeat it.

The entity spans are marked automatically by GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner], a pretrained NER model. Its multilingual version is used because the posts mix two languages. Marking every span by hand takes much longer than choosing one category, and the annotators have time only for the categories. The automatic annotation pipeline of HUMAID-NER cannot be reused, because it relies on an English language model and on rules written for English [@ali2026humaidner]. GLiNER is used without further training on the posts of the study, with the settings in @tbl-gliner-settings.

The models are trained on the training set with LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl], a library of multi-task optimizers. @tbl-training-settings lists the training settings, and @tbl-optimizer-setup lists how each optimizer is set up. Two of the settings, a batch size of 8 and an embedding layer that is not trained in any model, allow every optimizer to fit in the 8 GB of GPU memory of the laptop.

Every model is trained for 10 epochs, each of which is one pass over the training set [@warner2025modernbert]. After each epoch, the model is scored on the validation set, and the version of the model from the epoch with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary]. The validation score of a multi-task model is the mean of its two F1-scores, and that of a single-task model is the F1-score of its task, following HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. Early stopping, which ends training once the validation score stops rising, is not used, because a comparison of multi-task optimizers should give every model the same amount of training [@xin2022mtohelp]. Class weights and oversampling are not applied either, so that the losses remain those of HUMAID-NER and the optimizer stays the only difference among the candidate multi-task models.

The learning rate, which sets the size of each update to a model, is tuned for each model, as in the reviewed comparisons of multi-task optimizers [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. Each model is trained once with random seed 0 at each of the learning rates 1, 3, 5, and 8 × 10^−5^ [@warner2025modernbert], and the rate with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. For linear scalarization, the task weights are tuned together with the learning rate, over the values in @tbl-training-settings [@xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization].

Each model is then trained in five main runs with random seeds 1 to 5. This number is within the range of two to ten runs used in the reviewed comparisons of multi-task optimizers [@kurin2022unitary; @lin2023libmtl; @royer2023scalarization]. A random seed fixes the random choices of a run, so runs with the same seed process the training posts in the same order, regardless of the model. A run that fails, such as one that runs out of GPU memory, is repeated once with the same seed. When it fails again, the failure and its cause are reported, and the training setup is not changed for that optimizer.

A sample size based on resource constraints may not be large enough [@lakens2022sample]. To check this, each single-task model is also trained on 25%, 50%, and 75% of the training set. The resulting learning curve shows how the F1-scores change as more training posts are used [@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. The single-task models are used because a curve from a model that learns one task alone is not affected by the choice of multi-task optimizer. Each subset keeps the same proportions of the humanitarian categories, and a model is trained on it with seeds 1 to 5.

## Statistical Treatment

Each result is reported as the mean and sample standard deviation across the five main runs of a model. The first research question is answered with the F1-scores of the single-task models on the test set. The second is answered with the dataset and the multi-task model themselves, together with the Cohen's kappa of each batch of annotation. The third is answered with the F1-scores, relative changes, training time, and peak memory of the 13 candidate multi-task models. The F1-scores and relative changes of the candidate multi-task models are computed on the validation set, because the test set is reserved for the final multi-task model and the single-task models.

The final multi-task model is also selected on the validation set. For each of the 13 candidate multi-task models, $\Delta_{\text{MTL}}$ is averaged over the five runs, and the optimizer with the highest mean is used for the final multi-task model. When two optimizers have the same mean, the one with the shorter training time is selected. Among the five runs of the final multi-task model, the run with the highest validation score is used in the prototype and in the error analysis.

The fourth research question is answered on the test set, where the final multi-task model is compared with the single-task models. The hypotheses of Chapter 1 are tested with a two-sided paired t-test on the F1-scores, run once for each task. This test is appropriate because each run of the final multi-task model is paired by random seed with the single-task run that processed the training posts in the same order. The test examines whether the mean of the five differences in F1-score is zero, and the null hypothesis is rejected when $p$ is below .05. The mean difference is reported with its 95% confidence interval. The F1-score of each humanitarian category and each entity type is also reported, together with its number of posts in the test set. Training time and peak memory are compared through their means and standard deviations, without a statistical test.

## Data Analysis

The learning curve is used to judge whether the 2,500 posts are sufficient. It is interpreted by comparing adjacent training sizes, following Tabuzo et al. [-@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner], who considered a training size sufficient once a larger size no longer produced a significant gain in F1-score. This study compares the two largest sizes, 75% and 100% of the training set, because this step shows whether the F1-scores are still rising when the whole training set is used. The increase in the mean F1-score on the validation set from 75% to 100% is counted as a gain when it exceeds the standard deviation of the single-task model across its five main runs, which represents the usual variation between runs. Such a gain indicates that more posts would likely raise the F1-scores further, and this result is reported as a limitation. A smaller increase indicates that the F1-scores have stopped improving and that the 2,500 posts are sufficient. The curve of each task is interpreted separately, so the limitation may apply to one task and not the other.

The F1-scores of the final multi-task model are judged by how much they differ from those of the single-task models. No minimum acceptable F1-score is set, because no earlier study reports F1-scores for both tasks on Taglish posts about tropical cyclones. The errors of the final multi-task model are then analyzed to show which posts it labels incorrectly and why. No difficult posts are added to the test set on purpose, so the errors reflect the kinds of posts that the model is meant to label. For humanitarian classification, a confusion matrix shows how often each category is mistaken for each of the other categories. For NER, each incorrect span is classified by entity type and by type of error, which is a missed span, an extra span, or a span with incorrect boundaries or an incorrect type. The posts with errors are then examined together to identify what they have in common, such as their length, their mix of Tagalog and English, or their category.

## Software System Description

### System Structure

The software of the study consists of two systems, shown in @fig-system-architecture. The benchmarking system produces the dataset and the final multi-task model. The prototype web application uses the final multi-task model to label a stream of test posts and shows them to a responder on a map and in a table. Both systems run on the laptop of the study, and the X API is used only to collect the posts of the dataset.

The benchmarking system has six parts. Post collection requests the posts from the X API (Section 3.5). Post cleaning applies the inclusion and exclusion criteria, which include the removal of duplicates, and replaces personal details with placeholders (Sections 3.3 and 3.5). Post annotation uses doccano, in which the annotators assign the humanitarian categories, and GLiNER, which marks the entity spans. The dataset holds the annotated posts in their training, validation, and test sets. Model training and evaluation trains the 15 models and measures their F1-scores, training time, and peak memory. The trained models are stored with these measurements, and the final multi-task model is taken from them.

The prototype web application has five parts. The post stream replays the posts of the test set one after another, as if they were arriving during a tropical cyclone. Test posts are used because the final multi-task model has not seen them in training and because replaying them needs no connection to the X API. The server, built with FastAPI, holds the final multi-task model and labels each arriving post with its humanitarian category and its entities. It then looks up each LOCATION entity in the place list, a stored list of Philippine provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays with their coordinates, to find where the post belongs on the map. A post whose location is not in the list, or matches more than one place, is not placed on the map and appears only in the table. The server stores each post with its labels and coordinates in the database, which is PostgreSQL. The web interface, built with React, runs in a web browser and shows the stored posts on a map and in a table. The map is drawn from a stored file of Philippine boundaries, so no part of the prototype sends posts to an outside service.

![System Architecture of the Benchmarking System and the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-1-system-architecture.pdf){#fig-system-architecture}

### Use Cases

The prototype is a minimum viable product. It is not a complete system for disaster response, but it has the features needed to demonstrate how the labels of the final multi-task model could support decisions on where help and resources are needed. Each use case is one feature that the responder can perform. @fig-use-cases shows the eight use cases, and @tbl-usecases describes them. The responder is the only actor, because the stream of posts is already connected and needs no action from a user. The prototype is designed for responders, but it is not deployed or tested with them (Section 3.9). The final multi-task model only suggests the category and the entities of each post, and the responder decides which posts to act on, so an error of the model does not become a final decision.

![Use Case Diagram of the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-2-use-cases.pdf){#fig-use-cases}

| Use Case | Description |
|:--------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| View posts on a map | The responder can see the labeled posts as points on a map of the Philippines, each placed by the LOCATION entity of the post. |
| View posts in a table | The responder can see the labeled posts in a table, each with its time, its text, its humanitarian category, and its entities. |
| View the details of a post | The responder can select a point on the map or a row of the table to see the full text of the post, with each entity highlighted by entity type. |
| Filter posts by category | The responder can select one or more humanitarian categories, so that the map and the table show only the posts of those categories. |
| Filter posts by entity type | The responder can select one or more entity types, so that the map and the table show only the posts that contain an entity of those types. |
| Filter posts by location | The responder can select a province, city, or municipality, so that the map and the table show only the posts placed there. |
| Search posts by keyword | The responder can type a word or phrase, so that the map and the table show only the posts whose text contains it. |
| View a summary of posts | The responder can see the number of posts in each humanitarian category and in each province, city, or municipality, which shows where requests and reports are concentrated. |

## Testing and Evaluation

This section presents the test plan for the software of the study. Testing checks that the software works as designed. It does not measure how well the dataset is annotated or how well the final multi-task model performs. These are evaluated through the agreement between the annotators (Section 3.4) and the comparison of the final multi-task model with the single-task models on the test set (Sections 3.6 and 3.7).

The test plan covers both systems in @fig-system-architecture. For the benchmarking system, it covers every step that produces the dataset or a result, from the collection and cleaning of the posts to the scores, the training cost, the statistical tests, and the 13 multi-task optimizers. For the prototype, it covers the connections between its parts, the eight use cases in @tbl-usecases, and the labeling of the post stream. The usability of the prototype, its performance on other computers, and its use by actual responders are outside the plan, because the prototype only demonstrates the final multi-task model (Section 1.8).

Testing has three levels, which move from the smallest parts of the software to the whole system. @tbl-tests summarizes them. Unit testing and integration testing are automated with pytest, so that every test can be run again after any change. Functional testing is done by hand with written test cases, because its results are read from the screen.

| Test Level | What Is Tested | How It Is Tested | When | Pass Criterion |
|:-------------|:----------------|:------------------|:-------------|:----------------|
| Unit testing | Each part of the benchmarking system | Automated tests on small examples with known outputs | November 2026 to January 2027 | Every output matches its expected output |
| Integration testing | The connections between the parts of both systems | Automated tests on the practice batches and on constructed posts | Before the tuning runs and after the prototype is built | Every actual result matches its expected result |
| Functional testing | The eight use cases of the prototype and its labeling of the post stream | Written test cases run by hand with constructed posts | After the prototype is built | Every actual result matches its expected result |

: Test Plan Summary {#tbl-tests tbl-colwidths="[16,22,24,16,22]"}

Unit testing runs each part of the benchmarking system on small examples whose correct output is worked out by hand, starting with the parts that prepare the data, before the sample is collected. Appendix D lists each unit test. Integration testing then checks each arrow of @fig-system-architecture, with the posts of the practice batches for the benchmarking system and six constructed posts for the prototype. The practice batches pass through every part of the benchmarking system but are not part of the sample, so the test set is not seen before the final evaluation. Appendix E lists each integration test. When any test fails, the part is fixed and all the tests are run again, and the tuning runs start only after every test passes.

Functional testing starts once the prototype is built. Each of the eight use cases has at least one test case. Two more test cases check the post stream, one of them by comparing its labels with those of the evaluation. The test cases of the use cases run on six constructed posts with fixed labels, so that the expected result of every step is known in advance. Appendix F lists each test case with its step, expected result, and actual result. A use case passes when the actual result matches the expected result in every one of its test cases. When a test case fails, the prototype is fixed and every test case of that use case is run again.

@tbl-roles lists the role of each member of the research group. The tests are written and run by a member who does not develop the software, so that the software is not checked only by those who built it.
